narrative:
The model predicts you have a 47% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help you graduate.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your plans for higher education, your history of past failures, and the amount of time you study each week. Wanting to pursue higher education is actually the strongest influence, but in your case it works against you because you are the only student in the entire group who said you do not want to continue studying after this year. Almost every student who passed expressed a clear desire for higher education, so your answer pulled the prediction sharply toward failure.

Your clean record of zero past class failures was the second most important factor and pushed the prediction in the opposite direction, helping protect your chances. However, this positive effect was not enough to overcome the other influences. The third key factor was your study time. You currently study less than two hours per week, while most students who passed dedicate two to five hours. This lower study commitment also nudged the outcome toward failing.

To improve, the clearest steps are to rethink your longer-term goals and protect time for regular study. Even small increases in weekly study, combined with a realistic plan for what comes after school, could meaningfully change your trajectory.
